title: IAM Access Analyzer: findings worth fixing this sprint
excerpt: Access Analyzer will drown you in noise if you treat every finding equally. Here is the short list I fix first — and the ones I deliberately defer.
content:
IAM Access Analyzer is one of the highest-signal free controls AWS ships. It is also easy to ignore after the first hundred "external access" findings on a sandbox account.

I do not try to zero the backlog in a weekend. I triage. Here is the order that has paid off.

---

## Turn it on correctly first

- Enable an analyzer at the **organization** level if you can — account-level only misses cross-account trust you care about.
- Use unused access analysis where available; "who can reach this" and "who never used this" are different questions.
- Tag findings with account type (`prod`, `shared-services`, `sandbox`) so filters are not tribal knowledge.

If Analyzer is only on in one account, you are flying half-blind.

---

## Fix this sprint

### 1. Public access you did not mean

S3 buckets, SQS queues, SNS topics, KMS keys, and Lambda resource policies with `Principal: "*"` and no restrictive condition. Especially anything with `s3:GetObject` or decrypt permissions.

These are the findings that show up in breach write-ups. Fix or document a business reason with an expiry date — not a Slack shrug.

### 2. Cross-account trust to unknown or personal accounts

Roles that trust an account id nobody recognizes, a departed vendor, or a personal AWS account from a hackathon. Pull CloudTrail for `AssumeRole` on that trust. If unused, delete. If used, rotate to a known org account and MFA-conditioned assume where appropriate.

### 3. Unused IAM roles and users with powerful policies

Admin-adjacent principals with no activity in 90+ days are free real estate for attackers who land credentials from an old CI secret. Disable access keys, detach policies, then delete after a freeze window.

### 4. Resource policies that grant `*` actions to a whole account

`Principal: { AWS: "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:root" }` with `Action: "*"` on a bucket or key. Even "our" accounts should get least privilege — account root in a resource policy is a blunt instrument.

---

## Ticket this month (not panic)

- Public access on intentionally public assets (static websites, public datasets) — confirm the policy matches intent, add MFA delete / versioning where relevant, move on.
- Cross-account read access between known org accounts that is broader than needed — tighten ARNs and conditions, but schedule it; do not page.
- Unused access findings on read-only roles in non-prod — batch cleanup.

---

## Defer with a documented reason

- Findings on ephemeral sandbox accounts with no customer data and auto-nuke tags
- Known third-party integrations (Cloudflare, Datadog, GitHub OIDC) that Analyzer flags as external — verify condition keys (`token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub`, source IP, etc.) are correct, then archive
- Duplicate findings that are the same root cause across regions — fix once, archive the rest

Archive is not ignore. Archive with a link to the ticket or runbook. Silent archives are how public buckets survive reorgs.

---

## A simple weekly loop

```
Monday:  new critical/high external-access findings → owners assigned
Wednesday: unused privileged principals → disable keys
Friday:  archive review — anything older than 30 days needs a reason or a fix date
```

Wire EventBridge on Access Analyzer findings to Slack for severity high+, same pattern as GuardDuty. If nobody sees new findings within a day, the tool is decoration.

---

## What "done" looks like

Not zero findings. Zero *unexplained* public and cross-account findings on production accounts, and a shrinking set of unused privileged identities.

Access Analyzer will not design your IAM for you. It will tell you where your intentions and your policies diverged. Fix the divergence where it hurts — public data and powerful unused credentials — before you polish the rest.
